p: Paul opens with his chains, not his title. It is the only letter of his that does this.
b: Desmios means a man in bonds, a prisoner. In most of his letters Paul names himself "an apostle," the title of authority (2 Corinthians 1:1; Ephesians 1:1). Here he drops it. J. B. Lightfoot noted that Paul wants to ask, not command (1:8-9), and that a letter "penned within prison walls" is hard to refuse. The genitive "of Christ Jesus" can mean that Christ is the reason for the chains, or that Paul belongs to Christ as his prisoner. The word comes back in 1:9, and the chains in 1:10 and 1:13. One later copyist missed the point: the first hand of Codex Claromontanus (D, a Greek-Latin manuscript of the 400s or 500s) wrote "apostle" instead (see the variant).

p: Timothy is named beside Paul, as in several letters. He had worked with Paul in Ephesus, near Colossae.
b: Timothy appears in the opening of 2 Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians and both letters to the Thessalonians. Acts places him with Paul during the long stay at Ephesus (Acts 19:22), which is about the time, on Lightfoot's reading, that Philemon worked beside Paul. "Our brother" is family language: Paul calls Philemon "brother" (1:7, 1:20), Apphia "our sister" (1:2) and Onesimus "a much-loved brother" (1:16). In Greek adelphos is a brother; the plural adelphoi, used elsewhere for whole churches, includes women. Even so, the letter speaks in Paul's own voice ("I") from 1:4 on, so Timothy is a witness to the request rather than its author.

p: A believer with a house big enough for a church, and at least one slave. Colossians puts him at Colossae.
b: All that we know of Philemon comes from this letter. He owned a house where a church met (1:2), he had a slave, Onesimus (1:16), and he had been helped to faith by Paul, since Paul says he owes him "your own self" (1:19). Colossians says that Onesimus comes from Colossae and sends a message to Archippus (Colossians 4:9; Colossians 4:17), so most readers place Philemon there, a town in Phrygia in the Lycus valley. "Fellow worker" suggests he had once worked beside Paul, perhaps when Paul was at Ephesus (Acts 19:10). Lightfoot points out that the name had a local echo: in the old Phrygian tale of Philemon and Baucis, an aged couple welcomed gods unawares, and the people of Lystra in Phrygia's neighbor Lycaonia once took Paul and Barnabas for the same two gods (Acts 14:11-12).

p: Apphia is a local name found on many inscriptions in Phrygia. She was probably, but not certainly, Philemon's wife.
b: Lightfoot showed that Apphia is not the Roman name Appia but a native Phrygian name, found on inscriptions in town after town of the region. Because her name stands between Philemon and Archippus, many readers since the early church have taken her to be Philemon's wife, and Archippus their son. The letter does not say so: this is a guess. If she ran the household with Philemon, the matter of a household slave concerned her as well, which may be why she is named. Some later Greek copies of the subscription call Philemon and Apphia the "masters of Onesimus." Paul calls her "our sister," a fellow believer, and she is one of the few women named as the recipient of a New Testament letter.

p: Colossians gives Archippus a charge: finish the service he received. One theory makes him Onesimus's real owner.
b: Colossians 4:17 ends with a message for Archippus: see that you complete the service you received in the Lord. "Fellow soldier" is a picture Paul uses for a partner in hard work for the good news (Philippians 2:25). Readers have made Archippus Philemon's son (Lightfoot thought it likely) or a church leader. John Knox (Philemon among the Letters of Paul, 1935) argued that Archippus was the owner of Onesimus and that the "service" of Colossians 4:17 was to release him to Paul. Few have followed him. Later church tradition made Archippus a bishop: the Apostolic Constitutions (7.46) names him bishop of Laodicea.

a: the church that meets in your house
p: The first churches met in homes. The "your" is singular: the house belongs to Philemon.
b: The Greek reads "the church at your house" (kat' oikon; the site renders it "the church that meets in your house", as at Romans 16:5 and 1 Corinthians 16:19), with "your" in the singular. For the first two centuries believers met in private homes: Prisca and Aquila hosted one ("Greet also the church that meets in their house," Romans 16:5), Nympha another (Colossians 4:15), and Mary the mother of John Mark had a house where many prayed (Acts 12:12). There is no clear evidence of buildings set apart for worship before the 200s. This matters for the letter. Onesimus would come back not only to a household but to a congregation that met in it, and the slave, his master and the master's guests would share one table. The letter was meant to be read aloud there, so the whole church would hear what Paul asked.

t: A greeting to all of them
p: Here "you" is plural, the whole house church. From the next verse on, "you" is Philemon alone.
b: Paul's usual greeting joins the Greek charis, "grace," to the Jewish shalom, "peace." The wording is the same as Ephesians 1:2, so this site gives it the same English. The "you" here is plural (hymin): Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church. In 1:4-21 the "you" is singular, Philemon himself, and in 1:22 and 1:25 it turns plural again. The letter is a private request made in public, which put friendly pressure on Philemon.

a: when I speak of you in my prayers
p: From here to 1:21 every "you" is singular. Paul is now speaking to Philemon himself.
b: The phrase is literally "making mention of you in my prayers," the way ancient letters spoke of remembering someone before the gods. Paul's letters often open with thanks to God for the readers (Romans 1:8-9; 1 Corinthians 1:4). Here the "you" (sou) is singular, and it stays singular until 1:21. English "you" hides this. Readers should hear the letter as a word to one man, spoken while his household and church listen.

a: your love, and about the faith you hold toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints
p: Love comes first, then faith; then faith's object, then love's. The order makes an X pattern.
b: The sentence names love, then faith, then the Lord Jesus (whom faith looks to), then the saints (whom love serves). This crossed order, A-B-B-A, is called a chiasm. Lightfoot explained it this way: Paul's first thought is Philemon's love, which reminds him of the faith it comes from, which needs its object, Jesus; and then he finishes the first thought, love for all the saints. He also noticed that Paul changes prepositions: pros, "toward," for the Lord, and eis, "to," for the saints; some good copies read eis in both places (see the variant). Some copies smooth the order to "faith and love," which Lightfoot called "an obvious emendation." Colossians 1:4 has the plain order. Love is the letter's key word (1:5, 1:7, 1:9, 1:16).
orig: τὴν ἀγάπην καὶ τὴν πίστιν (tēn agapēn kai tēn pistin)

t: One of the hardest verses in Paul
p: Every word of this prayer can be read more than one way. The key word is koinonia, sharing.
b: Koinōnia means sharing, partnership, fellowship. Lightfoot listed the main readings: (1) the generous sharing that grows out of Philemon's faith, his gifts to others (as in Romans 15:26 and 2 Corinthians 9:13, where the word means a gift); (2) Philemon's fellowship with God through faith; (3) the sharing of his faith with others, by example; (4) his partnership with Paul in the faith, which Chrysostom favored because of 1:17 ("if you count me as your partner"). The Plain English Translation keeps "partnership in the faith" so that the link to 1:17 stays visible. The goal is that this sharing will become active "as you come to know fully" (en epignōsei) every good thing believers have, and so lead toward Christ.
orig: ἡ κοινωνία τῆς πίστεώς σου (hē koinōnia tēs pisteōs sou)

p: The Greek says active, at work. The old Latin read a word one letter different: "evident."
b: Energēs means active, effective, in working order; Robertson notes the papyri use it of a mill that works. The Latin translations render it evidens or manifesta, "plain to see," which shows that the Latin translators read enargēs, a word only one letter different. Lightfoot points out that Jerome, commenting on the verse, gives evidens as the Latin reading and efficax, "effective," as the Greek. Every Greek edition prints energēs, and so does the Plain English Translation.

p: Splanchna are the inner organs, the gut, where Greeks felt deep emotion. The KJV says "bowels."
b: Splanchna are the inner parts of the body: heart, lungs, liver. Greek speakers felt strong feeling there, much as English speakers feel it "in the gut." The KJV's "bowels of the saints" is literal but misleads today; "hearts" gives the sense. The word comes three times in this short letter: Philemon has set the saints' hearts at rest (1:7); Onesimus is Paul's "own heart" (1:12); and Paul asks Philemon to set his heart at rest (1:20). The verb "set at rest" (anapauō) is the one used of Titus in 2 Corinthians 7:13 ("his spirit has been set at rest by all of you") and means relief, a breathing space. Philemon's past kindness, perhaps gifts or hospitality for the church in his house, is the ground of the request that follows.

t: I could order you, but I won't
p: Parrhesia is the freedom to speak plainly. Paul says he has it, then sets it aside.
b: Parrhēsia was the citizen's right to speak freely in the assembly, and so frankness, boldness. Paul says that "in Christ" he has every right to give orders (epitassein) about "what is fitting" (to anēkon, a duty), and then chooses to appeal instead (1:9). The move is itself persuasion. Ancient teachers of speech called the speaker's standing his ēthos and the stirring of feeling pathos, and both are at work here: Paul reminds Philemon of his authority, his age, his chains and his love before he names Onesimus. F. Forrester Church read the letter as a speech of advice built by these rules (1978).

p: Not Philemon's love or Paul's, but love itself, as a claim that asks to be honored.
b: "Because of love" is literally "through the love" (dia tēn agapēn). Lightfoot argued that it means neither Philemon's love (1:5, 1:7) nor Paul's, but love as a principle that has a claim on both men. The contrast with "give you orders" (1:8) runs through the letter: Paul could command, but he wants a free act (1:14), and in the end he says he is sure Philemon will obey (1:21). The tension between asking and commanding is part of the letter's force.

p: The Greek reads presbytēs, "old man." Some scholars think Paul meant presbeutēs, "ambassador."
b: Every edition in this site's Greek word list (NA28, SBL, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text) prints presbytēs, "an old man." The word for "ambassador" is presbeutēs, one letter longer, and Ephesians 6:20 says "It is for this that I am an ambassador in a chain." Reading "ambassador" here is a conjecture, a change proposed without a manuscript behind it: Richard Bentley and others suggested it, and J. N. Birdsall studied it again (1993). Lightfoot believed Paul does mean "ambassador," but argued that no change is needed, since in Paul's time the two spellings were used for each other: Greek manuscripts of 1 and 2 Maccabees and 2 Chronicles 32:31 write presbytēs where the meaning is "ambassador." Laurence Welborn defends "old man" (2025) and, from ancient evidence about age, estimates that Paul was about sixty. The English versions this site checks against (KJV, ASV, YLT, WEB, BSB) all read "aged." The Plain English Translation follows the word as it stands, which means "an old man," and keeps the Greek's "now ... also" (nyni de kai), which adds the prisoner's chains to his age. Lightfoot himself noted that "old" and "prisoner" "would suit either entreaty or command," so the choice rests on the word, not on the appeal.

a: whom I fathered in my chains
p: Paul calls a convert his child, the way Jewish teachers spoke of pupils. Onesimus came to faith while Paul was chained.
b: Paul uses birth language for the people he brought to faith: "It was in Christ Jesus, through the good news, that I fathered you" (1 Corinthians 4:15), and "My children, I am in labor pains for you all over again" (Galatians 4:19). The verb is gennaō, "to father." So Onesimus became a believer through Paul, and while Paul was a prisoner, which made him, as Lightfoot put it, the child of Paul's sorrows. Paul also calls Timothy his child (1 Corinthians 4:17). If Philemon also owed his faith to Paul (1:19), the slave and the master are now brothers with the same father.
orig: ὃν ἐγέννησα ἐν τοῖς δεσμοῖς (hon egennēsa en tois desmois)

p: Paul praises, appeals and calls him "my child" before he names him. Onesimus means "useful."
b: In the Greek, the name is the very last word of the sentence, and Chrysostom pointed out that Paul holds it back until he has made Philemon ready to hear it. Onesimus (Onēsimos) means "useful" or "profitable," a name that, as Lightfoot notes, was very often given to slaves. The next verse plays on it. Colossians 4:9 calls him a faithful and beloved brother from Colossae itself, and sends him home with Tychicus.

a: Once he was useless to you. Now he is useful
p: Achrēstos, "useless," and euchrēstos, "useful," play on the name Onesimus, "Useful."
b: Paul writes achrēstos, "no use," and euchrēstos, "of good use." Neither word is the name itself, but both mean the same as onēsimos: the slave named Useful had been useless, and now lives up to his name. Lightfoot compared Naomi's "Don't call me Naomi. Call me Mara" (Ruth 1:20), another play on a name's meaning. Some readers also hear a pun on Christos, since chrēstos ("good, useful") and Christos sounded alike in Greek of the time: useless without Christ, useful in him. Lightfoot thought this too subtle to be likely. "To you and to me" says that the change benefits master and apostle both, and "to me" sounds like an afterthought, since Greek usually puts "me" first.

t: The Torah says: do not send him back
p: Deuteronomy forbids handing a runaway slave back to his master. Paul sends Onesimus back. How do these fit?
b: The Torah says: "Do not hand a slave over to his master when he has escaped from his master to you" (Deuteronomy 23:15). Most ancient law did the opposite. The rabbis read the law in several ways: a slave who fled from abroad into the land of Israel (Rashi, from Talmud Gittin 45a), a slave sold to an owner outside the land, or one bought in order to be freed. Paul, a Jew trained in the Torah, sends Onesimus back. Three points matter. Paul is not handing him over to punishment but asking that he be received "as if he were me" (1:17). The letter may not be about a runaway at all (see the deep dive on the chapter page). And Paul says he would have liked to keep him, but would not act without Philemon's consent (1:13-14). Readers still differ on whether Paul kept the spirit of Deuteronomy or set it aside.

p: Splanchna again. Greek and Latin could use it for one's own child; the Syriac Bible takes it that way here.
b: The word is splanchna, as in 1:7 and 1:20. It usually means the seat of feeling, so "my very heart." But Greek writers used splanchna, and Latin writers viscera, for a man's own children, and Lightfoot notes that the old Syriac translation, the Peshitta, renders it here as "my son." That would echo "my own child" in 1:10. Lightfoot preferred "heart," because Paul's other uses of the word are about feeling (1:7, 1:20). Either way Paul is sending a part of himself.

p: Paul says Onesimus could serve him for Philemon, as if Philemon himself were helping.
b: Hyper sou, "for you, on your behalf." Lightfoot noted the tact: Paul assumes that Philemon would have wanted to help his teacher in prison himself, and that a slave of his household serving Paul would count as Philemon's own service. The verb is diakoneō, to serve or minister, the word used for serving at table and for church service. Some readers think Paul is hinting that Onesimus be sent back to him (see 1:21). The imperfect "I had wanted" (eboulomēn) marks a wish he did not act on.
orig: ὑπὲρ σοῦ μοι διακονῇ (hyper sou moi diakonē)

a: the chains I wear for the good news
p: "The good news" is the word behind "gospel." Paul wears his chains because of it.
b: The Greek reads "in the chains of the good news" (tou euangeliou). Euangelion means good news, and is the word that English Bibles render "gospel." The chains are those that the good news brought on him: he is in prison for preaching it (compare Philippians 1:7, 13). Lightfoot noted that Paul wears them as a badge of honor and also as a reason for pity, and that Ignatius of Antioch, a bishop taken to Rome in chains early in the next century, spoke of his own chains in the same two ways.
orig: ἐν τοῖς δεσμοῖς τοῦ εὐαγγελίου (en tois desmois tou euangeliou)

p: Pliny, pleading for a freedman, worried his letter would look like an order. Paul has the same worry.
b: Paul did not want Philemon's "good deed" to be done "as if" forced (hōs kata anankēn), but "willingly" (kata hekousion). Lightfoot set this beside a letter of Pliny the Younger, a Roman senator writing a generation or two later, to his friend Sabinianus for a freedman who had angered him (Letters 9.21). Pliny writes that he is afraid he will seem not to ask but to compel. Pliny's letter worked: in Letters 9.24 he thanks Sabinianus for taking the man back into his household and favor. The two letters are the closest ancient parallels to each other, and the differences matter: Pliny's man is a freed slave who comes in tears to beg, while Paul calls Onesimus his child and a brother, and offers to pay.

p: Paul uses a passive verb, "he was separated," and leaves open who did the separating.
b: Echōristhē means "he was separated" or "he was parted." Chrysostom noticed that Paul does not say "he ran away" but "he was parted," a gentler word, and passive, as if the departure were not Onesimus's own plan. He compared Joseph telling his brothers that "God sent me here before you to keep people alive" (Genesis 45:5). The passive leaves room for God's hand without claiming it outright, which is why Paul begins with "Perhaps." The Plain English Translation keeps the passive. It is also the main clue for the view that Onesimus was a runaway, though the word does not prove it.

p: "For an hour" against "eternal": a brief absence set against a bond that will not end.
b: The Greek contrasts pros hōran, literally "for an hour," a short while, with aiōnion, "eternal," "for all time." Lightfoot argued that "eternal" should not be watered down: Onesimus had gained eternal life, so the bond between him and Philemon would now outlast death. The verb "have back" (apechō) is a business word for receiving payment in full, which fits the account language of 1:17-19.

a: have him back for all time
t: Claude's theory: "forever," but not as a slave
p: The Torah's slave who stayed "forever" stayed a slave. Paul's "forever" ends the slavery. A reversal?
b: This is my own reading. In the Torah a slave who chose to stay with his master had his ear pierced, and "Then he will serve him for life" (Exodus 21:6); Deuteronomy 15:17 says "he will be your slave for life." The Greek Old Testament reads eis ton aiōna, "forever," in both places. Paul tells Philemon that he will have Onesimus aiōnion, "forever," and then at once adds "no longer as a slave" (1:16). A reader who knew the Greek law would hear the old phrase turned around: the man comes back forever, but as a brother. Paul does not quote these laws, and the word aiōnios is common, so this is a possible echo, not a proof. Lightfoot stresses the eternal sense of the word; the link to the ear-piercing law is my own.

a: no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave
t: What does "no longer as a slave" mean?
p: Free in law, or a brother while still a slave? Paul's "as" leaves room for both, and readers have split.
b: Paul writes "no longer as a slave" (hōs doulon), not simply "no longer a slave." A change of standing within the church: Lightfoot held that Onesimus might still be a slave in law but could no longer be treated as one, since in Christ he was a brother; that "no longer" (ouketi) states a fact, "whether Philemon chooses to recognise it or not." Chrysostom read it this way too, and so did John Wesley, whose note on the verse reads "In the flesh - As a dutiful servant. In the Lord - As a fellow-Christian." (Wesley's introduction adds that "It seems, Philemon not only pardoned, but gave him his liberty; seeing Ignatius makes mention of him, as succeeding Timotheus at Ephesus." That is an inference from later history, not from this verse.) A request for freedom: others take "more than a slave" and "go beyond what I say" (1:21) as a hint that Philemon should free him (see the note on 1:21). Not a slave at all: Albert Barnes argued that nothing proves Onesimus was a slave, and Allen Callahan that he was Philemon's estranged brother. The card on the chapter page gives the churches' answers.

p: A doulos was owned by another person. The KJV's "servant" softens it; this site writes "slave."
b: Doulos is a slave: a person owned by another, who could be bought, sold, beaten and inherited. The KJV and some modern versions write "servant" or "bondservant," which can make readers think of hired help. Roman slavery was not based on race. People became slaves through war, kidnapping, debt or birth to a slave mother. Many slaves in cities worked in households and trades, and many were later freed, but their bodies were at the master's disposal, and cruelty was common. Paul also calls himself a slave of Christ (Romans 1:1). On how the slaves and masters of the churches were told to live, see Ephesians 6:5-9 and its card.

a: in the flesh and in the Lord alike
p: "In the flesh" is ordinary human life; "in the Lord" is life in Christ. Onesimus is a brother in both.
b: En sarki, "in the flesh," here means ordinary human life and relations, not sin. Lightfoot quoted the German commentator Meyer: in the flesh Philemon had the brother for a slave; in the Lord he had the slave for a brother. Paul goes further: Onesimus is to be a brother to Philemon "in the flesh" too, that is, in daily life in the household. Allen Callahan reads "in the flesh" as a blood tie: Onesimus and Philemon were brothers by birth. Most scholars take it as the everyday sphere, as in Ephesians 6:5, where slaves are told to obey their masters "according to the flesh."
orig: καὶ ἐν σαρκὶ καὶ ἐν κυρίῳ (kai en sarki kai en kyriō)

a: welcome him as if he were me
t: Receive him as you would receive me
p: The same verb as Romans 15:7: "welcome one another, just as Christ welcomed you."
b: The command, held back since 1:12, finally comes. Proslambanomai is to take someone into one's home or circle. Paul uses it in Romans: "So welcome one another, just as Christ welcomed you, for God's glory" (Romans 15:7). The word "partner" (koinōnos) picks up the "partnership" of 1:6: a business word for people who share a common venture. If Paul and Philemon are partners, Onesimus comes as Paul's representative. Luther read the verse as a picture of Christ, who takes the sinner's place before the Father; Lightfoot quotes his preface: Paul "setteth himself as if he were Onesimus."
orig: προσλαβοῦ αὐτὸν ὡς ἐμέ (proslabou auton hōs eme)

a: If he has wronged you in any way
t: Theft, a debt, or something else?
p: Paul says "if." Chrysostom says Onesimus stole and ran. Others think of a loss, a debt, or lost work.
b: Paul puts it as a condition: if he has wronged you, or owes you. Theft: Chrysostom says plainly that Onesimus "having stolen something from his master, had run away." Lightfoot agreed that the words probably point to a real wrong, and noted that Paul avoids the plain word "stole." Loss of work: any absence of a slave cost his owner money, so the debt may simply be the time he was gone. A dispute: on the amicus domini reading (see the chapter page), Onesimus had caused some loss and went to his master's friend to plead for him. The text does not settle it; what is clear is that Paul takes the cost on himself.

p: Ellogaō is a bookkeeping word: enter it in the account. Paul turns a letter of love into a business promise.
b: Ellogaō means to enter a sum in an account. Robertson notes that the word is known from inscriptions and papyri, and in the New Testament only here and in Romans 5:13 ("But with no law there, sin is not counted"). Paul uses a run of business words: partner (1:17), owe (1:18), charge (1:18), repay (1:19), owe besides (1:19). Christian readers have long heard in it a picture of the gospel: Luther, as Lightfoot quotes him, said "Even as Christ did for us with God the Father, thus also doth St Paul for Onesimus with Philemon.... We are all his Onesimi." The Byzantine text spells the verb ellogei, with no change of meaning.

p: "I, Paul, write this" is the form of a signature on a bond. Paul signs an IOU inside his letter.
b: Ancient contracts and receipts were signed with "I, so-and-so," and the past tense "I wrote" was the normal form of a signature. Paul writes "I, Paul, have written it in my own hand: I myself will repay," which reads like a signed note of debt. Elsewhere Paul dictated his letters to a scribe and added a few lines in his own hand at the end ("Look at the big letters I am using as I write to you in my own hand," Galatians 6:11; 1 Corinthians 16:21). Lightfoot thought the remark here shows that Paul wrote this whole short letter himself, which would be unusual. Others think he took the pen only at this point.
orig: ἐγὼ Παῦλος ἔγραψα τῇ ἐμῇ χειρί, ἐγὼ ἀποτίσω (egō Paulos egrapsa tē emē cheiri, egō apotisō)

a: you owe me your own self
p: Paul says he won't mention it, and so mentions it: Philemon owes Paul his very life in Christ.
b: "I need not tell you" (hina mē legō soi) is the device called paralipsis: saying something by saying you will not say it. Prosopheileis means "you owe besides" or "you owe in addition." Paul has just offered to pay Onesimus's debt; now he reminds Philemon that the larger debt runs the other way, since Philemon came to faith through Paul. Lightfoot compared Plato, who taught that a child owes his parents everything he has. A spiritual father could claim the same. The line is playful, and also firm.

a: let me gain something from you
p: Onaimēn, "may I have profit," is the verb from which the name Onesimus comes.
b: Onaimēn is a wish form of oninēmi, "to benefit," the root of the name Onēsimos. Paul has asked Philemon to receive the man named Profit; now he asks that he himself may profit from Philemon. Lightfoot noted that the phrase was often used of the return a parent hopes for from a child, and thought the play on the name "not unlikely"; Robertson agrees. The Plain English Translation keeps the money word "gain" so that the reader feels the business language still running.

t: Claude's theory: the three hearts are the argument
p: Philemon refreshed hearts (1:7); Onesimus is Paul's heart (1:12); refresh my heart (1:20). The chain makes the request.
b: This is my own reading. Robertson notes that splanchna comes three times in the letter. I think the three uses form the argument in small. In 1:7 Philemon is the man who sets the saints' hearts at rest. In 1:12 Onesimus is Paul's own heart. In 1:20 Paul asks Philemon to set his heart at rest. Put together: you are known for refreshing hearts; this man is my heart; so refresh my heart by receiving him. The verb "set at rest" also joins 1:7 and 1:20. Robertson notes the repeated word; reading the three uses as the argument is my own.

t: "Even more than I say": what more?
p: Paul does not spell it out. Freedom for Onesimus? Sending him back to Paul? A warm welcome? Readers differ.
b: Paul writes that he is sure Philemon will obey (hypakoē), and do "even beyond" (hyper) what he asks. Freedom: many readers think Paul is hinting at manumission. Lightfoot wrote that the word emancipation "seems to be trembling on his lips, and yet he does not once utter it." Return to Paul: others link the hint to 1:13, where Paul wished to keep Onesimus to serve him; John Knox thought this was the request. Welcome: others think of forgiveness and a generous welcome, without either. The word "obey" is strong after so much gentle asking, and shows that Paul's request was not optional.
orig: καὶ ὑπὲρ ἃ λέγω ποιήσεις (kai hyper ha legō poiēseis)

a: have a guest room ready for me
t: A guest room, and where Paul was held
p: Paul expects to visit soon. That suggests a prison near Colossae, such as Ephesus, rather than far-off Rome.
b: Xenia is lodging for a guest, a room in a private house or an inn. Lightfoot saw "a gentle compulsion" in the request: Paul would soon see for himself how Onesimus had been received. The request also bears on where Paul was writing. Rome: the ancient subscriptions to the letter, and Lightfoot, say Rome, where Acts shows Paul under guard for two years (Acts 28:16, 30). But Rome is far from Colossae, and in Romans 15:24 Paul had meant to go on west to Spain. Ephesus: Ephesus is close to Colossae, Paul suffered there (1 Corinthians 15:32; 2 Corinthians 1:8), and a short visit would be easy. Acts records no prison stay at Ephesus. Caesarea: Acts 24:27 has Paul held there two years. The chapter page sets out the views.
r: Acts 28:16; Acts 28:30; Acts 24:27; Romans 15:24; 1 Corinthians 15:32; 2 Corinthians 1:8; Philippians 2:24

a: given to all of you as a gift
p: Charizomai means to give as a favor. Paul hopes God will answer the church's prayers by releasing him.
b: Charisthēsomai is "I will be granted" or "given as a gift," from the same root as charis, grace. The passive leaves God as the giver. Lightfoot noted that the same verb is used of handing a person over to be killed (Acts 25:11) or to be saved (Acts 3:14); here it means release. "Your prayers" and "to you" are plural again: the whole house church is praying for Paul, and he will be their gift, not Philemon's alone.

p: Epaphras brought the good news to Colossae. He is named first because Philemon knew him best.
b: Colossians calls Epaphras "one of you" and the one from whom the Colossians learned the good news, a man who works hard in prayer for Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis (Colossians 1:7; 4:12-13). Lightfoot reasoned that Paul names him first in the greetings because he was a Colossian and the founder of their church, and so the best known to Philemon. He should not be confused with Epaphroditus, the messenger of the church at Philippi (Philippians 2:25).

a: my fellow captive in Christ Jesus
p: Synaichmalōtos means a fellow prisoner of war. In jail with Paul, or a captive of Christ like him?
b: Synaichmalōtos is built on aichmalōtos, a captive taken with the spear, a prisoner of war. Paul uses it of Andronicus and Junia ("fellow prisoners," Romans 16:7) and, in Colossians 4:10, of Aristarchus rather than Epaphras. Some take it literally: Epaphras shared Paul's prison at the time, perhaps by choice. Others take it as a picture, like "fellow soldier" (1:2): all of them are Christ's captives in his campaign. Robertson leaned toward the picture. The swap of the title between Epaphras here and Aristarchus in Colossians may mean that friends took turns staying with Paul.

p: Paul once refused to take Mark along. Now Mark is one of his fellow workers.
b: This is John Mark of Acts, whose mother's house in Jerusalem was a meeting place (Acts 12:12). He left Paul and Barnabas partway through their first journey, and Paul later refused to take him again, so that "Barnabas took Mark along and set sail for Cyprus" (Acts 15:39). Here he is among Paul's fellow workers, and Colossians 4:10 calls him the cousin of Barnabas and tells the church to welcome him. 2 Timothy 4:11 has Paul ask for him because he is useful (euchrēstos, the very word of 1:11) for service. In a letter about receiving back a man who had once been useless and is now useful, the presence of Mark is a quiet example of the same thing.
r: Acts 12:12; Acts 12:25; Acts 15:37-39; Colossians 4:10; 2 Timothy 4:11; 1 Peter 5:13

p: A Macedonian who was dragged into the riot at Ephesus and sailed with Paul toward Rome.
b: Acts names Aristarchus among Paul's companions seized in the theater riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:29), among those who traveled with him toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:4), and on the ship that took Paul toward Rome: "Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us" (Acts 27:2). Colossians 4:10-11 calls him Paul's fellow captive and counts him, with Mark and Jesus Justus, among the only Jewish believers working with Paul. His presence in both Ephesus and Rome means he cannot settle where Paul was writing.

p: Two Gentile coworkers. Later, Luke stays with Paul and Demas leaves him.
b: Colossians 4:14 sends greetings from Luke, the beloved physician, and from Demas. Lightfoot noted that Colossians counts Demas and Luke among Paul's Gentile coworkers (Colossians 4:11, 14). Their later paths part: in 2 Timothy 4:10-11, Demas has left Paul out of love for this world, and Luke alone is still with him. From the late 100s, church writers named this Luke as the author of the Gospel of Luke and of Acts. Jesus called Justus, greeted in Colossians 4:11, is not named here; Lightfoot guessed he was a Roman believer unknown to Philemon.

p: The blessing is for all of them together: "your" is plural, and they share one "spirit."
b: The letter ends as Galatians does ("may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen," Galatians 6:18). The "your" is plural (hymōn), so the blessing is for Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church in the house, and it would include Onesimus, now a brother among them. "Spirit" here is the human spirit, the inner life of each, spoken of in the singular as one.
orig: μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν (meta tou pneumatos hymōn)
